Pretty much you can't get away with discussing this book without at least referencing the movie. The film (which I admit did prompt me to read the book) is in hindsight a perfect documentary for the millennial, ADHD generation: Christian Bale, Ryan Gosling, Steve Carrell, Margot Robbie for 2 minutes (sans much of her awesome body, fully on display for the fappers in The Wolf of Wall Street), Brad Pitt, Selena Gomez, Jenga, whining that everything's going to be blamed on immigrants and poor people, and the insertion of a personal crisis for one of the lead "characters", and jump cuts left and right to make it all seem "authentic".

It also works as a decent summary for the book, not that the book is really that hard to understand. Lewis is ex-Wall Street himself, which isn't unusual, but he left early enough and developed his writing enough so that when he came to write this story of the guys who took on the house and won, he was able to put the concepts in a simple enough form. He is also smart enough to narrow the focus of his "history" to those few firms that saw the crash coming and did the rational thing and bet on it taking place. This makes the story easier to absorb.

This works both for and against his credibility in my view. While Lewis pillories those responsible in the private sector for Wall Street, he's not exactly objective or thorough in terms of history on the subject. At least he makes his biases obvious from the start: I recall an early quote where he speaks of Wall Street people paper-shuffling to "no obvious social purpose." Significantly absent in Lewis's discussion is any real acknowledgement of the policy settings or government decisions that allowed the subprime disaster to take place. Those would have taken a lot longer and would have involved criticising both Democrat and Republican governments for about the past forty years or so. On the other hand, criticising government is of limited benefit here since the network of incentives around subprime weren't that simple to detect and would take away the moral culpability of those who were responsible for the disaster ... that group of people being a very, very, very large pool of people who benefited ahead of the crash, and who would include a large body of property owners: the ones from whom the properties were bought with subprime mortgages.

The sense you get from Lewis's book is that the subprime collapse was not one body orchestrating the crisis. Quite the contrary, it's a number of very large institutions acting like absolute fuckwits. We are talking systemic failures by massive, well-heeled bodies, from ratings agencies to AiG to most of the big banks. Lewis expresses his anger against the players he sees responsible, but the humbling and staggering thing about the crisis is that it wasn't one or two people who caused the bubble. The entire system was rigged towards this result. It was like evolution in reverse: a culture developed where failure was not only possible, but inevitable. Nobody checked the viability of underlying mortgages on the bonds, mainly because the system was incentivised not to check them, and everyone was actually making money until someone asked the question. Imagine, if you will, the Titanic, but designed with a glass hull and with the boiler-stokers paid increasing amounts of money to get the ship to go faster and faster. Imagine a Titanic with two ship's lookouts who are competing with each other on how little risk their reports contain about the ice field the ship has entered. Imagine passengers taking bets on the Titanic not sinking even as it cruises happily into an ice field. That's essentially the financial system when the subprime crisis hit. I'm reminded of a motivational speaker's tape I once heard, which contained one penetrating point: "Your life can be a lot broader when you realise that everything around us that we call life was made up by people who are no smarter than you."

If nothing else, The Big Short reminds us that outsiders and newcomers to institutions, processes, cultures are important. They show us where the obvious problems and advantages of the system lie, because they aren't weighed down with the "accepted" way things are done. Michael Burry, basically acknowledged as the first guy to predict the collapse of the mortgage bond market, was not a Wall Street insider. Quite the opposite: Scion Capital, his investment firm, was based on the West Coast. Burry himself was, essentially, autistic: few other people had actually sat down and gone through the mortgages underlying the bonds he shorted, because there were literally thousands of them. He found it difficult to relate to people, but it also allowed him -- in this limited situation -- to cut through the bullshit of what people were saying about the bonds' security and what the position actually was.

The style is chatty and absorbable. If you've read Lorenzo Carcaterra's Sleepers you'll know the basic way the book's written: lots of street-ish talk combined with a few poignant sentences here and there for effect. At the very least reading this book educates you enough to then ask the question: what were the structural, policy reasons behind the collapse? Because nobody's really asking those questions, and as far as I can tell, nobody in the US government is really fixing the problem. The most significant thing is that most of the "heroes" of this story got the fuck out of this sort of investment. Burry famously closed Scion Capital and invested in "water" because he was pushed to the point of collapse by his investments, and some of the others outright got out of finance entirely. In essence, the film follows the book on the most important aspects of it. In other places, it still provides some surprises. It is well worth a look for a close-up picture of the machine as it went into collapse.
